bibliography.abstract: Cities need land for homes, shops, roads, and public services. New construction changes that land. It can harm natural areas and water bodies, add to waste, and strain public services. NITI Aayog's 2021 report stated that 65% of 7,933 urban settlements in India had no master plan. That number tells us about planning coverage at the time. It does not tell us whether any single building was authorised. Artificial intelligence, which lets computers learn patterns from data, can help find physical changes by comparing satellite images taken on different dates. We test simple methods on two public datasets from outside India. First, we turn each image into a set of numbers using a pretrained neural network, a model already trained to recognise patterns in images. We feed those numbers to standard machine-learning classifiers that predict land categories and physical changes. The methods reach about 95 percent accuracy at spotting built-up land and about 83 percent accuracy at saying whether a small pair of images shows change, where each pair gets one label. We also train a small neural network on a standard change-detection benchmark. Separately, we run a preliminary descriptive check on an Agra sample of 48 patches, 7 of them positive. The results show that satellite images carry information about physical change. They do not show whether construction was planned or permitted.
bibliography.title: Monitoring Unplanned Construction Using Satellite Change Detection

en.caveats: The evaluated methods detect physical land-cover modifications without distinguishing between legal, permitted developments and unauthorized construction.
en.what: The authors evaluated baseline land-cover classification and change-detection workflows using pretrained neural network embeddings alongside standard classifiers across two public satellite datasets, achieving 95% accuracy for built-up land identification and 83% accuracy for binary change detection at the image-pair level. A light neural network was also evaluated on a benchmark change dataset, accompanied by a small descriptive test on 48 image patches in Agra, India, which contained 7 positive change instances.
en.why: The results demonstrate that off-the-shelf satellite computer vision pipelines can reliably detect physical surface changes, though additional administrative data is required to determine if observed construction violates local planning regulations.
